---

It is common to live properly—to pretend you feel neither heat nor grief: to wave each night at Miss Fugue and Mister Goggles before diving into your nightcap, before reading yourself a bedtime story or watching your beloved sink to the bottom of a lake, then noting his absence in your log. The next day, you drop his clothes off at Goodwill like a sack of mail flung from a warplane, then hobble back to your hovel like a knight who moves only in Ls. What I am trying to say is that I think it is all right to accelerate around corners, to grunt back at the mailman, and to swallow all your laundry quarters. So much of everything is mere baffling nonsense: water extinguishes fire, my diseases can become your diseases, and two hounds will fight over a feather simply because feathers are strange. All I want is to finally take off my cowboy hat and show you my jeweled horns. If we slow dance, I will ask you not to tug on them—yet secretly I will want that very much.

---

outputs.L2: Living the right way is ordinary—acting as though you notice neither warmth nor sorrow: give an evening greeting to Miss Fugue and Mister Goggles before you plunge into your nightcap, before you tell yourself a bedtime tale or observe your darling drift down to a lake's floor and record his vanishing in your journal. Come morning, you deposit his garments at Goodwill the way you'd toss a mailbag from a fighter plane, then limp back to your shack like a chess knight that travels only in L-shapes. There's a coziness to existing this way, particularly in these times, yet it leaves you wide open to being startled—you overlook the mortgage payment and stumble upon a falconer's glove in your yard, an entire hand lingering within it. Or you return from an exhausting day to find your kids have abruptly turned repulsive and impossible to cherish. What I mean to convey is that I believe it's fine to speed up while rounding bends, to snarl in reply to the mailman and gulp down every quarter meant for your laundry. Nearly all of it is senseless deflection: fire yields to water, my sicknesses can pass into you and become yours, and a pair of dogs will battle over a single feather simply because feathers are peculiar. My one desire is to at last remove my cowboy hat and reveal my jeweled horns to you. Should we sway together in a slow dance, I'll request that you don't pull on them, though deep down I'll be craving exactly that.

# On Living Authentically

Living "properly," as society defines it, often demands that we suppress our most genuine emotions. The heat of passion and the depths of grief become inconvenient intrusions upon the orderly life we are expected to maintain. So we bury these feelings beneath the comfortable weight of routine and pretense, presenting a composed exterior while our truest responses to the world remain hidden, unexpressed, and quietly stifled.

Yet this manner of existing, however comfortable it may appear, comes at a significant cost. When we live at a distance from our own emotions—detached and carefully guarded—we render ourselves deeply vulnerable. The very shocks and disturbing surprises we sought to avoid strike us all the harder precisely because we have grown unaccustomed to feeling anything intensely. Our polished composure becomes brittle, and sudden disruptions can shatter what routine had so carefully protected.

Given this, perhaps there is wisdom in reconsidering what we so readily dismiss. It may, in fact, be acceptable—even necessary—to embrace behaviors we have learned to condemn: the irrational, the defiant, the unruly. To abandon decorum now and then, to act against expectation, might not be a failure of character but rather an honest acknowledgment of what it means to be fully alive.

After all, much of the world itself refuses to conform to reason. It operates through strange and senseless contradictions that resist every attempt at logical explanation. If existence itself is so often absurd and inconsistent, why should we demand a rigid coherence from ourselves that reality never demonstrates?

Beneath all of this lies a single, deep-seated longing. The speaker's greatest desire is not for order or approval, but for something far more intimate: to reveal the hidden, vulnerable true self that pretense has so long concealed—and, in that act of exposure, to be genuinely seen and intimately accepted by another. This, ultimately, is what makes the risk of authenticity worthwhile.
outputs.L4:
# Living Properly

There's a particular kind of safety in living properly. You wake at the same hour. You pour the coffee, answer the emails, nod at the neighbors. You keep the machinery of your days running smoothly, and in that smoothness, something inside you goes quiet. This is how the poem begins its exploration—not with dramatic sorrow, but with the practiced calm of someone who has learned to manage their grief by tucking it neatly beneath routine.

The speaker understands that emotional detachment can be a kind of medicine. When you've lost something, or someone, the disciplined structure of ordinary life becomes a way to survive. You don't cry at your desk. You don't let the ache surface. You maintain. You cope. And for a while, this works. The numbness feels almost like peace.

But the poem reveals the paradox hidden in this arrangement. The very comfort of suppression—the careful smoothing over of every rough edge—leaves the heart unguarded in a strange way. When you have trained yourself to feel nothing, you are utterly unprepared for the moments that break through anyway: a familiar song, an unexpected scent, a stranger's laugh that sounds like someone gone. These small things arrive like sudden shocks, jarring precisely because you'd forgotten how to brace against feeling. The armor of routine, it turns out, protects you from everything except the thing that matters most.

And so the poem turns. It stops defending the quiet life and begins to yearn for something rawer and more honest. Rather than continuing to suppress the storm inside, the speaker begins to wonder what it would mean to embrace the chaos instead—to stop performing composure and to let the true, hidden self rise to the surface. There is a longing here: not just to feel, but to be *seen* feeling. To reveal the messy, aching, complicated person beneath the well-managed exterior.

This is where the poem finds its courage. It acknowledges the fear—the terrible vulnerability of exposure, of showing someone who you really are when you've spent so long hiding. To be authentic is to risk being hurt, rejected, misunderstood. Yet the poem insists that this risk is worth taking. Real connection, the kind that reaches all the way in, requires that we drop our defenses and offer our unguarded selves to another.

In the end, the poem is a quiet act of rebellion against the anesthetized life. It chooses the trembling honesty of vulnerability over the safe deadness of "living properly." It reaches toward intimacy despite the fear, arguing that a life fully felt—chaos and grief and tenderness alike—is far more alive than one carefully arranged to feel nothing at all.

# The Fugue of Miss and Mister

Every morning at precisely nine o'clock, **Miss** Eleanor Hartwell sat down at her piano and began to play a **fugue** by Bach. The interweaving melodies filled her small apartment, each voice chasing the last, layering upon one another until the room seemed to breathe with music.

Across the hall lived **Mister** Thomas Reed, a quiet clockmaker who had never learned to play a single note. Yet every morning, he would pause his careful work, tilt his head, and listen through the thin walls. The fugue became the rhythm of his days—the counterpoint to his ticking clocks, the harmony that guided his patient hands.

For months, they never spoke. **Miss** Hartwell did not know that anyone listened, and **Mister** Reed could not summon the courage to knock. The music was their only conversation, a dialogue conducted entirely through walls and wood and the mathematics of Baroque melody.

Then one gray autumn morning, the fugue did not come.

**Mister** Reed waited. Nine o'clock passed. Then ten. The silence pressed against him like a held breath. Worried, he crossed the hall and knocked—the first time in all those months.

When **Miss** Hartwell opened the door, pale and surprised, he simply said, "I missed your fugue this morning."

She smiled, understanding at last that her private music had never truly been alone. "Would you like to come in," she asked, "and hear it played?"

And so the two voices, like the melodies in Bach's great compositions, finally found their way to one another—separate lines at last woven into a single, unexpected song.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about the strange comfort of routine and the desire to be truly seen by someone you love.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Arithmetic of Being Known

Every morning I fold myself into the same three minutes: coffee darkening, the window's grey light, the cat's insistence. I have learned to love the groove worn smooth by my own passing, the way a river loves its banks even as it dreams of the sea.

There is a safety in the clockwork. The bread knows my hand. The stairs remember the exact weight of my descending. I am a small god of small returns, presiding over the liturgy of the kettle, the sacrament of the unmade bed made again.

But listen—

Sometimes at night I want to be excavated. To have someone reach past the reliable surface of me, past the woman who always laughs at that part of the movie, who always leaves the last bite, and find the trembling animal underneath, still wet from its own becoming.

You watch me pour the milk and think you know the story. And you do—you know *a* story, the one I perform so well it has become almost true. But there is another me, folded like a letter never sent, addressed in a handwriting even I have forgotten how to read.

Come closer. Undo me like a knot you're patient with.

I am tired of being fluent in myself. I want to stammer in your gaze, to be a language you're still learning, to be surprised by what you find when you turn me over in your hands like a stone you've carried for years and only now hold up to the light.

The routine says: *you are safe, you are known, you are the sum of your Tuesdays.*

But love, I am asking the impossible—

hold me the way the morning holds the coffee's steam:

briefly, completely,

as though I were the only warmth

worth watching disappear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of experimental writing that blends absurdist imagery, grief, and intimacy—include odd characters, dark humor, and a vulnerable confession at the end.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Taxidermist's Guide to Leaving

The mailman delivers only weather now. Today: a fistful of drizzle, damp and apologetic, which I sign for with my mother's maiden name because my own has been discontinued, like a flavor nobody bought.

I keep her in the freezer. Not my mother—the *feeling*. I labeled it in wax pencil: GRIEF, DO NOT THAW. It sits between the peas and a fish I named Gerald, who died of my inattention and now judges me with one frostbitten eye.

---

Mr. Pinwheel comes Tuesdays to wind my clocks, though I own no clocks. He winds the air instead, cranking his invisible key while the silence gets tighter, tighter, until the room hums like a held breath.

"You're leaking again," he says, tapping my sternum.

I am. Something clear and saltish. I've been leaking since the funeral, where I laughed at the wrong moment—when the priest said *she has gone to a better place* and I pictured Cleveland. She hated Cleveland. She would've haunted me for the mispricing of her afterlife.

Mr. Pinwheel doesn't laugh. He collects laughter in mason jars and sells it back to the grieving at a markup. Business, he says, is *dead*. Then he winks like it's the funniest thing, and maybe it is, maybe everything is, maybe the whole architecture of loss is just God's stand-up routine and we're the crowd that forgot how to leave.

---

The woman I love is made mostly of doorways.

You walk through her and end up somewhere warmer. I did this once. I stepped through her collarbone and found a kitchen where my mother was still alive, still burning toast, still saying *you'll understand when you're older* about everything, about all of it, about the toast.

"You can't stay," the doorway-woman whispered. "I'm not a house. I'm just a place you pass through on the way to admitting things."

---

So here's the thing I've been not-saying, packed in ice, labeled and mislabeled:

I don't miss her cleanly. That's the confession. Grief was supposed to be a cathedral and instead it's a cluttered garage—half sorrow, half relief, a rusted bicycle of anger nobody's touched in years. Some mornings I forget she's gone and reach for the phone, and some mornings I remember and feel *lighter*, and I hate that lightness more than any weight, because what kind of son floats?

I laughed at the funeral because I was afraid. That's all. I was afraid that if I started making the other sound, the true one, it would never stop, it would empty me like a drain, and I'd be nothing but a wet name and a mailman with more weather.

So I froze it. I named the fish. I let Mr. Pinwheel wind the empty air.

But it's Tuesday. And the ice is melting. And I think—God, I think I'm finally ready to make the other sound.

I loved her. I didn't always like her. I would give my whole discontinued name to burn toast beside her one more time.

There. It's thawing now.

Let it flood.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of contemporary surrealist poets like Matthew Zapruder or James Tate, addressing the reader as "you" and building toward a tender, bizarre image.
counterfactuals.output:
Instructions for Assembling the Evening

You wake to find the day
has been folded wrong,
one corner tucked beneath
the other so the afternoon
shows through the morning
like a stamp held to a lamp.

This is normal. Everyone
does this now. The mail carrier
told me so, delivering
a single white glove
and a letter addressed
to the person you almost were.

You should open it.
Inside there is a small weather,
a private drizzle
you can keep in your shirt pocket
and take out when the meetings
grow too bright.

I know you are tired.
I know the refrigerator hums
a song your mother hummed
and you can't remember
if that's a comfort or a wound,
and honestly neither can I.

But listen: tonight
when you lie down
and the ceiling pretends
to be a ceiling,
I want you to imagine
I have come to your door

holding a lamp made
entirely of the sound
a dog makes when it dreams,
and I am saying,
gently, in the voice
you use for no one—

here, you forgot this,
you left it years ago
on the last good afternoon,
this warm and breathing thing
that fits, impossibly,
exactly in your hands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a stream-of-consciousness prose poem that starts with mundane domestic life and spirals into unsettling, dreamlike scenarios before arriving at a longing for connection.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Kettle Never Boils the Same Way Twice

The kettle is doing that thing again, that low insistent hum before the whistle, and I'm counting the tiles above the sink, seventeen and a half if you include the one the previous tenant cracked, and the milk needs using up, the milk always needs using up, there is a permanent condition of milk in this house, milk and unopened envelopes and the particular Tuesday quality of light that means nothing has happened and nothing will—

but the tiles, if I count them again, there are nineteen now, and the sink has grown deeper, the way sinks do when you look away, and my hands are in the water and the water is warm and then it is a lake and then it is the memory of a lake, the one from childhood that may not have existed, where my mother stood at the edge in a dress the color of dishwater calling a name that isn't mine—

and the kettle is still not boiling, will never boil, has decided against boiling as a lifestyle, and I am walking down a corridor that used to be my hallway, past doors that were never here, and behind each one a version of me is setting a table for a guest who never comes, forks arranged like small silver ribs, and I want to knock but my knuckles pass through the wood like it's the idea of wood—

the ceiling is breathing. This is fine. The ceiling has always been breathing, softly, the way a house holds its inhabitants in its lungs, and I am so small now, I am the size of the space between what I meant to say and what I said, and there are people at the bottom of the stairs, I can hear them, laughing at something, and I would give the whole flooded kitchen, all nineteen tiles, the cracked one especially—

just to know their names, just to be handed a cup of something warm by someone who knows how I take it, to be the guest that comes, to knock and have the door swing open, to have a face turn toward me in a room and *soften*—

the kettle boils.

Someone should be here to hear it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a strange, funny, and heartbreaking poem about pretending to be normal while hiding your true monstrous self—end it with an image of secret horns and slow dancing.
counterfactuals.output:
**Passing**

I practice my smile in the bathroom mirror,
adjusting the teeth so they don't look too many.
I've learned to laugh at the right decibel,
to nod when someone says *nice weather*
even when I can smell the storm inside my ribs.

I buy the correct oat milk.
I say *how are you* and wait,
politely, for the lie
I know they'll give me back.

Nobody suspects the thing
that curls up sleeping in my chest cavity,
that I feed at 3 a.m. with grief and cold spaghetti.
Nobody knows my shadow doesn't match my body,
that it has an extra set of arms
it forgets to hide when I'm tired.

It's exhausting, being a person.
The paperwork of it. The eyebrows.
The way you have to keep your voice
from doing that low harmonic thing
that makes the dogs go quiet.

But then—
you found me at the party,
by the coats, half-hidden,
where I go to breathe like something feral.
And you said, *me too.*
And I said, *me too, what?*
And you reached up, gentle as a secret,
and touched the place beneath my hair
where the horns come in,
small and warm and terrible,
the ones I file down every morning
so the world won't run.

You didn't run.

You had your own, it turned out—
just below the left ear,
soft as new antlers, blunt from the same hiding.

So here we are,
two monsters in cardigans,
swaying in the coat closet
to a song we can't quite hear,
our secret horns
almost, almost
touching.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
